Meeting header:
Date: 2027-07-21
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Ava Chen (Redwood AE), Michael Ortiz (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood Solutions Eng); Raj Patel (CTO, Aurelius), Sofia Gomez (Head of Infra), Liam Brooks (ML Engineer), Maya Singh (Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect): Deep dive on private VPC networking patterns, PrivateLink, NAT, subnets, DNS; runtime impact notes on KV cache, batching and quantization. Next steps: share docs, run benchmarks.

[00:00] Ava Chen: Hey everyone, um, quick roll call, and then michael will jump into the network and runtime details.
[00:08] Raj Patel: Yep, hi, Raj here. Sofia, Liam and Maya are with me.
[00:12] Sofia Gomez: hi all, sofia here.
[00:14] Liam Brooks: Liam here.
[00:16] Michael Ortiz: Morning/afternoon from our side. I'm Michael, SE; I'm going to cover the Private VPC networking and then how that ties into runtime constraints.
[00:25] Jordan Lee: Jordan here for any infra IaC questions.

[00:30] Michael Ortiz: Alright, quick agenda: private connectivity (PrivateLink vs peering), egress patterns (NAT, gateway endpoints), subnet topology and AZ distribution, DNS and Route53 split-horizon, and then runtime notes: KV cache, batching, quantization and the latency/throughput tradeoffs. Questions as we go, please interrupt.

[01:02] Sofia Gomez: Quick context: we're locked down to VPC-only endpoints; no public internet egress for runtime nodes is allowed except to specific S3 buckets. We also need audit logs forwarded to our SIEM, and KMS usage for keys.
[01:18] Michael Ortiz: Got it. So that pushes us toward PrivateLink or VPC peering + strict route tables. PrivateLink gives you no public IPs on the runtime plane and the traffic doesn't traverse the public internet. The tradeoff is more setup on your side: endpoint service consumer permissions, and you need cross-account endpoint acceptance if it's across accounts.
[01:45] Raj Patel: Can you explain the difference in terms of performance and latency? We worry about added latency from PrivateLink.
[01:52] Michael Ortiz: Sure. In most regions we've measured p50 overhead of 1-2ms when using Interface Endpoints/PrivateLink versus direct public ingress, but the variability depends on the path your cloud provider takes. The bigger latency drivers are the model size, quantization path, and batching windows. PrivateLink itself is small compared to a 50-200ms model token generation. For low-latency use cases (p50 < 100ms) we recommend Dedicated capacity in the same AZs as your app or colocated gateway, and keep sequence lengths small or use prompt caching.
[02:33] Liam Brooks: Sequence length — we have both short chat style queries and longer summarization jobs (8k tokens). How does KV cache factor in?
[02:42] Michael Ortiz: KV cache stores key/value attention cache for autoregressive decoding. For chat with long histories, having the KV cache resident avoids recomputing prefixes and can reduce p99 latency for follow-on tokens substantially. On Private deployments we pin runtime nodes so their warm KV cache can persist per-session. For high-concurrency shorter prompts, batching helps throughput but can add tail latency. There's a tradeoff: increase batching window to amortize kernel startup cost versus latency tail.
[03:18] Maya Singh: From security: we require no public egress for model pull and image updates either, unless it's S3 via VPC gateway endpoints. Can Redwood support pulling models from our S3 using a gateway endpoint only?
[03:28] Jordan Lee: Yes, that's the usual pattern: provision a Gateway Endpoint for S3 in your VPC and use an IAM role to let the runtime nodes pull model artifacts. If you want PrivateLink for inference API, you can still have gateway endpoints for S3. Note: S3 gateway endpoints are regional and are fine for data plane model pulls. For container image registries, you may need ECR interface endpoints or a transient NAT for external registries depending on your registry choice.
[03:58] Sofia Gomez: What about NAT costs? We have budget concerns for NAT Gateway in each AZ.
[04:05] Michael Ortiz: Right, NAT Gateway costs can add up. Options: 1) NAT Gateway per AZ (simplest, highest cost), 2) central NAT with hairpinning via Transit GW (more complex), 3) use ECR/ECS private endpoints or mirror images into your private registry in VPC. For S3 model pulls, gateway endpoints mean no NAT costs. For telemetry forwarding to our hosted observability, you can configure VPC flow logs to a partner collector, or we can push audit logs over PrivateLink to your SIEM if you prefer.
[04:42] Raj Patel: You mentioned PrivateLink to send logs to our SIEM? How does that work?
[04:47] Michael Ortiz: We can expose an endpoint service for logs or metrics and you create an Interface Endpoint consuming it. That keeps logs on the AWS network. The other pattern is to have our agent/proxy send only metadata over PrivateLink and push full logs to your S3 via gateway endpoints. We can support both.
[05:06] Liam Brooks: For runtime performance, are there any ENI or throughput limits we need to be aware of?
[05:11] Jordan Lee: ENI limits per instance type do matter. For high-concurrency runtime nodes we recommend instance types with higher ENI/ENP limits; also consider jumbo MTU for optimized RPC in some regions. We'll share a recommended instance matrix.
[05:26] Michael Ortiz: Also, for KV cache and stateful sessions we rely on sticky routing to a runtime pool; that means flow affinity at the LB or endpoint. With PrivateLink you can get ENIs in your subnet and endpoints map to us — we still do sticky session routing on our side so the same user's session hits the same runtime shard where their KV cache is warm.
[05:52] Sofia Gomez: DNS — we run split-horizon Route53 private hosted zones. How should we handle the Redwood endpoint DNS?
[05:59] Michael Ortiz: Two patterns: 1) we give you the endpoint IPs and you create A-records in your private hosted zone that point at the endpoint ENIs; 2) we publish a private hosted zone that you associate with your VPC, or we provide a conditional forwarder. Many customers prefer the private hosted zone you manage so you have full control. Note: for failover across regions we provide fallback records and you can manage TTLs accordingly.
[06:28] Maya Singh: TLS termination — does Redwood terminate TLS at our PrivateLink ENI or do we terminate locally? Need to ensure we use our KMS.
[06:36] Michael Ortiz: We support mutual TLS to the endpoint. Termination options: we can terminate on our side with customer-provided certs (bring-your-own cert) and use KMS for encryption-at-rest, or you can terminate at your side and have a secure channel to Redwood's service IPs. For key management Redwood can integrate with your KMS for envelope encryption; we'll share the KMS integration doc.
[06:58] Raj Patel: Regarding quantization — how much latency improvement do you see moving from fp16 to int8 or 4-bit?
[07:06] Michael Ortiz: It depends on model and kernel maturity. For many transformer models, int8 gives ~1.6-2.2x token throughput improvement and reduced memory footprint which lets you fit larger KV caches or run larger batches. 4-bit (a16/q4 variants) can improve memory further but sometimes increases compute overhead depending on the kernel. There's also a small quality delta; we run evals on your prompt set to measure regression. Int8 is usually a sweet spot for production.
[07:40] Liam Brooks: If we quantize, do we need different model artifacts in S3?
[07:44] Jordan Lee: Yes, you'll typically store the quantized artifact separately. Our deployment tooling can pull the correct artifact based on the model pin or rollout rule. We recommend a naming scheme in S3 and lifecycle policies.
[07:56] Michael Ortiz: Also keep in mind cache warm-up: when you switch to a new model or quantized artifact, KV caches are invalidated and you may see a transient latency bump. We recommend canary rollouts across a small subset of instances to warm caches.
[08:12] Ava Chen: Quick interruption — what's your target SLO for inference latency and throughput? That helps us size Dedicated vs hosted.
[08:19] Raj Patel: For chat flows p50 < 200ms is ideal, p95 < 600ms. For batch summarization throughput is more important. Cost target is under $0.02 per 1k tokens if possible.
[08:33] Michael Ortiz: p50 < 200ms for chat with 2k tokens is doable with Dedicated and int8 quantization in-region. For p95 < 600ms you need careful batching windows and prefix caching. Token-cost targets depend on model size and batch; our Optimize tooling will recommend batching and cache configs to reach unit-cost goals.
[08:55] Liam Brooks: On batching, what are the knobs? We worry about tail latency.
[09:00] Michael Ortiz: Batching window and max batch size are the main runtime knobs. Also dynamic batching heuristics based on arrival rate. For latency-sensitive paths, we recommend small max batch sizes and short windows (e.g., 10-20ms), plus kernel-level optimizations like fused attention. For throughput jobs you can relax windows to 50-100ms to hit higher throughput.
[09:23] Sofia Gomez: Can you do hybrid: PrivateLink for inference, gateway endpoints for S3, and a central NAT for outbound telemetry?
[09:29] Jordan Lee: Yes, that's a common pattern. We typically see: PrivateLink interface endpoints in private subnets for inference API, S3 gateway endpoints for model/artifact pulls, ECR/VCR endpoints or mirrored images to avoid NAT, and either a central NAT for telemetry or PrivateLink for log ingestion. We'll include an architecture diagram in the docs.
[09:50] Raj Patel: For high availability across AZs, do you recommend endpoints in each AZ?
[09:55] Michael Ortiz: Yes. Create interface endpoints in each AZ/subnet where your app instances live and update route tables accordingly. For failover across regions we have fallback model variants in other regions but there's cross-region replication considerations for model artifacts and increased latency.
[10:12] Maya Singh: Auditing and compliance: We need audit logs with user-level tracing and retention for 12 months. Can Redwood ship audit logs to our S3 and also forward to Splunk?
[10:21] Michael Ortiz: We can. We support sending audit logs to customer S3 via gateway endpoints and can also push via PrivateLink to your SIEM. Retention policies can be applied on your S3. We also have SOC 2 artifacts; I'll attach our compliance pack.
[10:35] Ava Chen: Quick recap: Redwood to send PrivateLink checklist, Route53 pattern doc, KMS integration notes, and recommended instance/ENI matrix. Customer to share VPC CIDRs, AZ preferences, and sample workload. SE will run microbench and share spreadsheet. Any other asks?
[10:50] Liam Brooks: If you could include a sample IaC snippet for interface endpoint + endpoint service that would be super useful.
[10:57] Jordan Lee: We'll include Terraform and CloudFormation examples.

[11:05] (Crosstalk)
[11:08] Raj Patel: One more question on cost: if we do Dedicated reserved capacity, can we burst to hosted if capacity is full?
[11:14] Michael Ortiz: Yes. We have routing policies that allow fallback to hosted models in emergencies. You can choose whether fallback is allowed for sensitive data — for some customers we disable hosted fallback. For cost predictability we recommend reserved capacity with a burst pool.
[11:32] Ava Chen: Alright, we'll get those docs out. Thanks everyone.
[11:36] Sofia Gomez: Thanks, this was helpful.
[11:38] Liam Brooks: Thanks.
[11:39] Meeting end.
